records.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
records.author: sanchitmonga22
records.storyText:
Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

records.title: Show HN: Faros Desktop, a local app to see your AI traces and extend your usage
records.author: sachinag
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Sachin, and I’ve spent the last couple of months working on Faros Desktop, a Mac app that visualizes how you use your local AI coding tools into one place and then makes recommendations to make your subscription spend go further.

As agents have replaced hands-on-keyboard work, the team and I wanted to better understand what’s in our session traces. Faros Desktop hydrates with on-device session history in Codex, Claude Code, Github Copilot, and Cursor to let users deep dive into a beautiful visualization of AI session traces. Then based on consolidating that information, the app shows patterns in usage as well as recommendations for ways to save spend through simple changes that we call Power Ups.

Faros Desktop is totally free, with no login required and no API keys needed. The app also only uses on-device models to summarize local sessions in chunks, then organizes them by project and task. You can jump around a session timeline and see exactly the messages and tool calls in the trace.

The business model here for Faros Desktop is to drive thought leadership and create leads for our sales team to sell the company’s multi-player Token Engineering Platform for large engineering organizations. Faros has been serving large engineering organizations for the past seven years, so it was cool to be able to build a product for all Builders, not just enterprise engineering orgs.

One big direction we’re exploring: using previous sessions to make the next one better. We’re looking at local memory portability across harnesses as well as multi-player modes to share memory within your direct team. I’d love to hear thoughts on that.

records.title: Show HN: Tool to measure log TCO savings without losing or migrating any data
records.author: rinkash
records.storyText:
I work on Chiron. We provide a “lossless consolidation” solution for log savings on high-fidelity stores like Splunk, where you don’t lose any data, your query results stay intact, and you still meet your compliance needs. On a Palo Alto firewall log sample we published, the lossless merge came to about 40%. Method and numbers: https://medium.com/@chironvision_inc/keeping-palo-alto-logs-...

We built this estimator tool so that people can get a savings number on their own logs before they reach out to us. It is a binary tool with an MCP server plus a skill. Point your Claude, Cursor or similar at a local folder where your log sample is located. The tool produces a savings estimate report. It makes sure that no data leaves your network, and no data goes to your model either. The model only gets a statistical summary and metadata.

Install (or grab the tarball from the same path; checksums.txt is there, and releases are Sigstore signed):

curl -fsSL https://www.chironvision.com/dl/ea324478d02311d6b42f939c08b0... | bash -s -- --target claude

The tool comes with a zookeeper sample bundled so you can quickly test and validate the setup.

Currently supported log formats: Splunk exports, OTLP JSON, k8s container logs, plain text.

The detailed README on how to use the tool is included in the download.

How the tool works: it reads the logs from the provided folder or files and runs the analyzer to compute the lossless savings. The tool interacts via the MCP server with your Claude console or similar. You can run it from your Claude or Cursor console.

The engine is a binary, not open source; the license is at the download path.

Run the sample, then a few minutes of your own logs

records.title: Show HN: Natel, a Self-Hosted Google Contacts Alternative for CardDAV, 20MB RAM
records.author: Protectator
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I decided to move away from Google Contacts and self-host my contacts two months ago. After installing a Radicale server, I was really missing a way to edit my contacts on the desktop. Nextcloud is overkill for my needs, and InfCloud is the only other web contacts editor but it hasn't had a release in more than 10 years.

So I built what was the missing piece in my setup : Natel, a lightweight self-hosted contacts editor for a CardDAV server. The goal is to edit your contacts on the web, be robust enough to not make you lose anything when there's an edit conflict with the server, and be super light in resources on the server. I came up with building a docker image of just a proxy caddy server and a go process that stores your credentials only in-memory, for a compressed image of less than 30MB and it uses less than 20MB of RAM when idle.

Tested against four CardDAV servers : Nextcloud, Radicale, Baïkal and Xandikos. I already use it myself and it syncs with my server and DAVx5 back-and-forth, but I consider it still in beta and want to add more testing to prove compatibility for features I don't (yet ?) use. Note that any field that isn't displayed is never lost, it's just written back as-is.

Demo: https://demo.natel.app/contacts Website: https://natel.app

I wouldn't have done this side-project if I couldn't delegate writing the code to agents. We iterate on architectural decisions together, and once I'm satisfied with the direction, they write the result in a file (find it in docs/DECISIONS.md in the repo), then write the code to meet the expectations and independently review each other's iterations. I drive the project's direction and decisions, but I don't review the code myself. I keep an eye on the tests to know what's covered, and will read and review code when an agent draws my attention to it. The e2e tests were able to find a bug in SoGO, a CardDAV server : https://bugs.sogo.nu/view.php?id=6269 (and I didn't add that server in the compatilibity list yet because that bug breaks one the promises of the app, which is to be warned if we're trying to delete a contact that is modified elsewhere ; the server doesn't correctly enforce the If-Match instruction)

As I don't have that many users yet, I welcome feedback on any part of the project but especially the parts that I have not yet tested like Contacts on a Mac !

It's a new feature I've added to my app Pour Decision.

The idea is:

1. Set an interval on your phone and slip it in your pocket

tools/bench.sh downloads eight freely licensed recordings from Wikimedia Commons and repeats the FLAC and MP3 comparison against the FFmpeg you have installed.

Limits: the MP3 number is for a fast path (the exact path is slower than FFmpeg).

The code was written by an AI model (Claude) under my direction, nothing was accepted without a measurement. They're the decoders inside Orpheic, a free music player I'm building.

records.title: Show HN: Indexed_bzip2 2.0 – I used AI to make bzip2 decompression 4x faster
records.author: mxmlnkn
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I started indexed_bzip2 years ago as a seekable, parallelized bzip2 backend for ratarmount. It has been dormant for a while and seemed almost finished. Out of interest, I tried looking for bugs with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which found dozens of them, most with a minimal reproducing test. After reviewing and merging those and making a bugfix release, I prompted it with: "Speed up decompression by 2x". Surprisingly, it worked! You can try it out yourself with (timings on Ryzen 3900X):

    pip install indexed_bzip2==2.0  # Depending on your default: --uploaded-prior-to P0D, or uvx, pipx
    
    # single-threaded gzip decompression
    time igzip  -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.gz  | cksum  # 7.5 s
    time  gzip  -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.gz  | cksum  # 22.4 s
    
    # single-core bzip2
    time  bzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 105 s
    time lbzip2 -d -c -n 1 silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 77.6 s
    time ibzip2 -d -c -P 1 silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 23.7 s
    
    # parallelized
    time lbzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 6.7 s
    time ibzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 3.8 s

    # single-threaded compression
    time  igzip -c          silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 11.3 s
    time   gzip -c          silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 147 s
    time  bzip2 -c -z       silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 312 s
    time ibzip2 -c -z -P 1  silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 164 s
    
    # parallel compression
    time lbzip2 -z -c -n 24 silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 12.7 s
    time ibzip2 -z -c -P 24 silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 13.7 s
It not only added lots of dynamically dispatched SIMD code, ABI3 wheels, Trusted Publishing, all things I had long dreaded setting up, but also found libsais for an early inverse-BWT speedup. A contributor then used Claude Fable to replace libsais with an interleaved lane-walking inverse-BWT and SIMD symbol kernels, which hides the random pointer-chase latency and gave another 1.7x. The lane interleaving follows: Karkkainen, Juha, Dominik Kempa, and Simon J. Puglisi. "Slashing the time for BWT inversion." 2012 Data Compression Conference. IEEE.

ReadMe: https://github.com/mxmlnkn/librapidarchive/blob/HEAD/python/...

Benchmarks: https://github.com/mxmlnkn/librapidarchive/blob/HEAD/results...

records.title: Show HN: Infoboxing – Guess the Wikipedia article from its infobox
records.author: spykr
records.storyText:
I made a daily game where you try to identify five Wikipedia articles by looking at their infoboxes with the name and picture hidden. You get one guess per article, and afterwards you get a summary and a link to Wikipedia so at least you might learn something even if you get it wrong!

Infoboxing was inspired by the Wikipedia guessing game Catfishing, which my friends and I love. We play as a group, which is probably cheating, but still sometimes only get like 3/10 correct. Part of the fun is discovering each person's niche and comparing our answers to the rest of the Catfishing audience on the stats page.

I've always wanted to make a daily game and I felt there was still room to explore in the Wikipedia guessing space. In my first prototype I picked out four or five rows from each infobox and revealed them one at a time, but making someone guess repeatedly at something they may never have heard of felt slow, especially across five articles. I ended up following Catfishing's approach: show all the clues with one guess or a skip.

My fiancée and I choose the articles. We started out listing everything we could think of, then explored Wikipedia lists like the "Unusual articles" page and also used AI to suggest candidates in areas we'd missed. In my opinion the best articles have an "a-ha!" moment where it suddenly clicks.

The hardest parts to get right are article curation, balancing the difficulty and deciding what counts as a correct answer. Should "Big Jesus" be an accepted answer for Christ the Redeemer? My fiancée thinks so! I've also put in some rules to try and keep a given day from being too difficult but ultimately it's based on vibes because my idea of what "everyone knows" is biased by my age, gender, region, etc.

The infoboxes are captured ahead of time so I set up a daily check to warn me if an article changes, mainly to catch things like ages changing or people dying. My favourite facepalm moment was when it warned me that Spock had died. His date of death on Wikidata? 2263.

Anyway, give it a go and see what you think. If you have an answer you think should count, tell me through the contact page so that we can keep spoilers out of the comments.

records.storyText:
I built a flashcards app and plugin for obsidian, based on markdown syntax. You use headers and paragraphs, tables or highlighted text to create flashcards and cloze deletions, which you can then review using FSRS algorithm. Everything stays local, it uses a SQL lite db internally to keep track of state and keep the markdown document clean.

I started this project about a year ago when I was facing the problem that I needed flashcards to memorise thousands concepts and language vocabulary I kept forgetting and I hated every flashcards app out there so I decided to build something of my own and I started with markdown and obsidian. Fast forward one year later, I released the iOS and android apps too and a directory for ready made decks to share with people what Im learning, and also help other learners on their journey.

For me it was very interesting to build it because I had to come up with different conventions for what consists a flashcard while limiting myself only to markdown, so that the source text and the flashcard are one thing and they can be read also as a document, without custom syntax or delimiters cluttering it. Im still introducing new features as I explore new possibilities.

I built the foundations myself, algorithms, scheduler, parser. The part that was rough was finding a way to link headers to a state. At first Id just use the hash of the heading text to link it to the state in the database but that would break if you changed the text. So then I tried to use a string similarity algorithm to tie headings to same state, but that caused conflicts. In the end I ended up injecting a static ID on the heading body as a markdown comment. Obsidian hides it in live and reading views and it remains visible only in source mode view. Hate it from a purist perspective but it was a necessary compromise to guarantee a steady state that survives edits.

The app is free on android and as a plugin if you would like to try it. I charge a one time fee of 19.99 on iOS as a way to support the project, in a similar fashion to the Anki model.

records.title: Show HN: Crosshead - Working memory and persistent identity for agents
records.author: jbwinters
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

Have you ever been using Claude Code or Codex and run into a limit that ruined your flow? Claude says you’ve hit your limit but you’re knee deep in a refactor and want to keep going. Switching to Codex in that situation requires either having up-to-date handoff docs or rebuilding context from scratch. In both cases, you burn tokens just to handle moving context from one thread to another. Or maybe you have a great session, then compaction comes along and your agent forgets half of the important details.

I run into this a lot. Furthermore, I’m tired of one-off agents that can’t keep a stable identity across independent threads. I don’t want to be locked into Anthropic’s walled garden, or OpenAI’s ecosystem, I want to move freely as I see fit.

That’s why I built Crosshead. It’s more than a memory bank: it tracks the tasks, decisions and details that matter when work moves to a new thread. Your agent gets a stable cryptographic identity (a Nostr keypair) that carries across threads and tools, and handoffs are signed with it. Hooks inject context at each turn, so the agent always has the most important information available.

In my benchmarks of carrying task state into a new session, Crosshead passed 98% of fresh tasks, compared to 86% for claude-mem and 50% for Claude Code’s built-in memory. It also cost less per run than the other memory tools I tested, though built-in memory and a plain handoff file were a little cheaper. Details can be found here: https://crosshead.sh/benchmark

The catch is that it does not outperform when resuming the same session since caching is so cheap. Crosshead is best for people and agents who frequently encounter compactions, restarts, and harness/runtime switching. I am looking for folks interested in testing it with agents that are created and torn down frequently but need to retain context, like customer support or research agents.

It’s set up as a freemium service. Hot memory is free, and warm/cold memory is paid. I have added other features too, which are also paid via credits. You can purchase credits via Stripe or Lightning micropayments. The CLI and hooks are open source (https://github.com/FriendMachine/crosshead), and warm/cold memory and other features are hosted. Hot memory is synced first to a daemon on your machine then to the hosted service, so hot memory is also available offline. For other agents, there are native integrations for Hermes and OpenCode, an embeddable runtime for Pi agents, and an HTTP API. Show your agent https://crosshead.sh/skills/crosshead-bootstrap/SKILL.md to have it set itself up.

If you are interested in testing it, I recommend installing it in a single project first with

  curl -fsSL https://crosshead.sh/install | bash -s -- --add-to-path
  cd your-project
  crosshead quickstart --scope project --adapter both --api-base https://crosshead.sh --source-excerpts on
(The benchmark results depend on source excerpts, which is why the command turns them on. With them off Crosshead passed 50% of the main tasks. Excerpts are short pieces of the files and command output your agent reads. They sync to the hosted service in plaintext, not end-to-end encrypted, so leave the flag off if you are sensitive about sharing that.)

I am eager to hear your thoughts. I can imagine some of the pushback already, but you always surprise me with your critiques.

records.title: Show HN: Skjalf TV, Steam Deck native, controller-first IPTV player
records.author: ctbellmar
records.storyText:
I wanted to watch my IPTV subscription on the Steam Deck, both handheld and docked to a TV. But any existing option was either a desktop app or a Kodi setup (or worse, an Android emulator setup) that fought with Game Mode, so I wrote a player that treats the Deck as the main target.

It is purposefully simple. It plays live TV, movies, and series from your own Xtream Codes account or M3U playlist. It ships no channels or content. It doesn't have a ton of options - just the basics that are enough for my daily use, and perhaps yours too.

Some tech bits for others doing similar work:

- SteamOS has a read-only root filesystem and no libmpv. Instead of redistributing binaries, the installer downloads pinned mpv packages from Valve's own SteamOS package mirror, checks them against SHA-256 hashes in a lock file, and bundles the shared libraries into the user's home directory.

- Text entry in Game Mode: the app opens and closes the Steam on-screen keyboard through steam://open/keyboard, and reads properties of the Steam UI window on the X display to know whether the keyboard is showing. I did this to avoid rolling my own and to follow what worked well in Android apps. Bonus side effect is that your customized Steam keyboard appears here, rather than something generic.

- Video uses libmpv's render API to draw into an OpenGL framebuffer inside egui, so the video and the controller-driven UI share one window under gamescope.

- Some providers have catalogs of more than 180,000 movies and series. The app indexes them once and draws only the visible rows, so lists stay responsive on the Deck. Sorting (default and alphabetic) is there because providers often send seemingly random order.

- Arabic and Persian titles needed bidi reordering, because egui does not reorder right-to-left text on its own. Not super exhaustively tested but enough to make it workable.

- The installer adds the app to Steam as a non-Steam game by writing Steam's binary shortcuts.vdf with a stable app ID, so the library artwork shows up.

Install in Desktop Mode:

  `curl -fsSL https://github.com/bikemazzell/skjalf-tv/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh`
(yes, not everyone's fave approach, so the repo has releases you can download and deploy yourself and steps to build your own from source)

About 20,000 lines of Rust including tests, MIT licensed.

If it is of interest or usefulness to you, I appreciate feedback, especially from people who run it on other SteamOS devices. Thanks!
